cards.text: Jesus is still on the Mount of Olives, teaching His disciples, who came to Him privately (Matthew 24:3). He just told about ten virgins waiting for a bridegroom (Matthew 25:1-13), and now He gives another picture. It's just like a man going on a journey, who calls his servants and entrusts them with his possessions.

cards.question: The man gives one servant five talents, another two and another one. What decides how much each servant gets?

answers.text: How long each one has served

cards.text: Then the master leaves on his journey, and the five-talent servant goes at once and puts the money to work. No snooze button, no "I'll start Monday," just GO.

cards.question: The five-talent servant puts the money to work right away. What does he gain?
True or false: The servant with two talents also gains as much as he was given.

cards.text: Now the one-talent servant goes off on his own, and friend, this guy has a VERY different plan.

cards.question: What does the one-talent servant do with his master's money?

answers.text: Digs a hole and hides it
Gives it away to the poor

cards.question: True or false: The master of the servants comes back soon, before much time has passed.

cards.text: After a long time, the master comes back and settles accounts. The five-talent servant steps up first, presents five more talents and says, "See, I have gained five more."

cards.question: The master tells the five-talent servant he's been faithful with ___ things, so he'll be put in charge of ___ things.

cards.text: The master's reply opens with "Well done, good and faithful servant!" and ends with "Enter into the joy of your master!" Friend, if anybody ever said that to me, I'd frame it over the ovens and point at it EVERY. SINGLE. MORNING.

cards.question: The two-talent servant comes in with two more talents. How does the master's reply to him compare with what he told the five-talent servant?

answers.text: It's word for word the same
It comes with a stern warning

cards.text: Finally, the one-talent servant steps up and says, "Master, I knew that you are a hard man, reaping where you have not sown and gathering where you have not scattered seed." Opening your performance review by telling the boss what's wrong with HIM, friend, that is BOLD.

cards.question: The one-talent servant says he knew his master was a hard man. What does he say he was, because of that?

cards.text: So he hid the talent in the ground, and now he hands it back: "See, you have what belongs to you." That's like getting handed cookie dough to bake and bringing back the same lump with dirt on it, like "Good news, I didn't burn it!"

cards.question: True or false: The master is pleased that the one-talent servant kept his money safe in the ground.

cards.text: The master answers, "You wicked, lazy servant!" Then he points out that the servant knew he reaps where he has not sown.

cards.question: If the servant knew all that, what does the master say he should have done with the money?

cards.text: Then on his return, the master would have received it back with interest, and honestly, friend, with WAY less digging.

cards.question: The master orders the one talent taken from the lazy servant. Who does he say gets it?

answers.text: The one who has ten talents
The one who has four talents

cards.text: Then the master gives the reason: "For everyone who has will be given more, and he will have an abundance."

cards.question: True or false: The master says the one who does not have will get to keep what he has.
Last, the master orders the worthless servant thrown out. Where to?

cards.text: Out there, there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. That's where we'll leave this one for now, friend, but Jesus isn't done teaching yet.

findings.problem: This blank asks the baker to supply the master's exact wording, 'a few things' and 'many things', and the baker can't reason it out. Five talents is a large sum, so nothing on the earlier cards points to 'few'. A baker could also argue for 'risky' or 'hard' in the first blank, since the servant put the money to work.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The wrong word 'risky' (and arguably 'hard') fits the first blank believably. The five-talent servant did take a risk by putting the money to work, so a baker could argue it's right.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'It's shorter and much cooler' sounds slangy and a little silly. 'Cooler' can read as 'more awesome', and it doesn't match the tone of the other answers.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The comparison mixes the Bible setting into the everyday image. The dough comes back 'with dirt on it', which borrows the buried-in-the-ground detail instead of keeping to one cookie image.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: The joke mocks the servant for handing back an untouched, dirty lump of dough. That signals the master won't be pleased, which rules out 'True' on the next card (card 4) before the baker answers it.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Multiple choice makes up 4 of the stop's 6 choice cards. There are 2 true or false cards and no fill in the blank card, so one type dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.
